note: Read 2026-11-01 at the owner's word ("Build those first 3 starting with ledger first"; of the 21 countries read first: "It should cover across every country"; "Retry the blocked tax facts once all countries land"): the tax on a screen worker's pay in Singapore: a resident's income tax, social contributions, what is withheld at source, a non-resident artiste's withholding, an author's treatment, VAT and the tax year. Research and retry subagents (workbench/briefs/BRIEF-tax.md, BRIEF-tax-retry.md), every quote checked by the lead against its saved page.

figures.finding: A tax resident pays progressive income tax on chargeable income from 0% on the first $20,000 to 24% above $1,000,000 (rates from YA 2024 onwards, so for 2026 income assessed in YA 2027); there is no regional layer.

A Singapore citizen or permanent resident employee contributes 20% and the employer 17% of monthly ordinary wages to the CPF, up to an ordinary-wage ceiling of $8,000 (maximum $1,600 and $1,360 a month); foreigners do not contribute.
figures.applies: CPF members (citizens and PRs); age bands lower the rates for older workers (not read)

sources.said: Contributions are payable by Singapore citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (i.e. SPR obtained via immigration rules) only. Employers and employees contribute 17% and 20%, respectively, of monthly ordinary wages (OW), up to an OW ceiling of SGD 8,000. Their respective maximum contributions are therefore SGD 1,360 and SGD 1,600 per m

figures.finding: Singapore has no payroll withholding of income tax: a resident is assessed in the year after the income and pays within one month of the assessment (or by monthly GIRO instalments).

sources.said: Singapore does not have payroll withholding. … The tax assessed is payable within one month of the date of the assessment

figures.finding: A non-resident public entertainer has 15% withheld from taxable income for services performed in Singapore (the 10% concession lapsed after 31 March 2022), paid by the 15th of the second month; it is a final tax unless the entertainer qualifies as a resident. Other non-resident employment income is taxed at 15% or resident rates, whichever is higher.

value.base: taxable income from services performed in Singapore
value.remitBy: 15th of the second month after payment
value.nonResidentEmployment: higher of 15% flat or resident rates

figures.applies: Non-resident public entertainers (artistes, musicians and similar)

sources.said: A non-resident public entertainer is subject to a withholding tax of 15% on taxable income from services performed in Singapore. … The concessionary tax rate of 10% will lapse after 31 Mar 2022. From 1 Apr 2022, a withholding tax rate of 15% will apply on taxable income from services performed in Singapore. … pay the withholding tax to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment
Employment income of a non-resident individual is taxed at the flat rate of 15% or the progressive resident tax rates (see table above), whichever is the higher tax amount.
For public entertainers, this is a final tax unless they qualify to be taxed as Singapore tax residents.

figures.finding: Royalties paid to a non-resident bear 10% withholding as a final tax where the recipient has no business or PE in Singapore; no separate regime for a resident author was read.

sources.said: Royalty payments are subject to WHT at the rate of 10%. The tax withheld represents a final tax and applies only to non-residents that are not carrying on any business in Singapore and have no PE in Singapore.

figures.finding: A freelancer's fee bears GST at 9% once taxable supplies exceed $1 million in 12 months.

sources.said: GST is charged at 9% on the supply of goods and services made in Singapore by a taxable person … GST registration is required if a business makes taxable supplies in excess of SGD 1 million for a 12-month period.

figures.finding: The tax year is the calendar year; income of one year is assessed in the next (the year of assessment) and the return is due by 18 April.

sources.said: The tax year in Singapore is the calendar year. An individual’s income from a preceding calendar year is assessed to tax in the following calendar year (i.e. year of assessment). … The tax return must be filed on a calendar-year basis and must be submitted by 18 April.
